questions.prompt: A team is training a chess-playing agent that plays games against itself, receiving a reward for winning and a penalty for losing, with no dataset of labeled "correct moves" at all. Per Lesson 1, which paradigm is this, and why?
options: Reinforcement learning — the agent learns a policy from reward and penalty signals through repeated interaction with an environment, not from labeled correct-answer pairs
Supervised learning — the win/loss outcome is just a label applied to each move, the same as a spam/not-spam label
Unsupervised learning — the agent is finding structure in its own move history with no labels involved at all
It isn't a valid ML paradigm, since a model needs a labeled dataset to learn anything
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines reinforcement learning as an agent taking actions in an environment and learning a policy from reward and penalty signals rather than from a fixed dataset of (input, correct-output) pairs. A win or loss isn't attached to each individual move the way a label is attached to a supervised training example — the chess example in Lesson 1 specifically contrasts this with supervised learning's answer-key structure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 2, every time you call an LLM API to answer a question or summarize a document, the model's parameters are already frozen — you are doing pure ________, not training.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 points out that calling an LLM API is pure inference: the model was trained once, its parameters are frozen, and your request is one more forward pass through an already-finished model — exactly why a pretrained model can't "remember" earlier calls unless the application resends that context itself.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 3 term to what it actually is.
right: The near-universal split of a dataset into a 2-D table of inputs and a 1-D column of answers
An input column the model is allowed to use to make its prediction
A row's full set of feature values, with the label removed
The column holding the correct answer the model is trying to predict
questions.explain: A feature is one input column the model may use; the label is the column holding the correct answer it's trying to predict. A feature vector is a row's full set of feature values minus the label. Splitting a dataset into X (features) and y (labels) is the near-universal first step of supervised learning that Lesson 3 introduces.

questions.prompt: A model scores 0.99 on its training data and 0.61 on a held-out test set it never trained on. Per Lesson 4's diagnostic table, what does this gap indicate, and what's one general fix?
options: Overfitting — the model has memorized training-set noise rather than the generalizable pattern; a simpler model, more data, or regularization helps
Underfitting — the model is too simple to capture the real pattern; a more expressive model or more features helps
A good fit — any gap between train and test score is expected and not a problem worth addressing
The test set must be mislabeled, since a model that scores 0.99 on training data should score similarly everywhere else
questions.explain: Lesson 4's diagnostic table is explicit: a huge gap between a high training score and a much lower test score is the signature of overfitting, not underfitting (which shows both scores mediocre with no gap). The general fixes for overfitting are a simpler model, more training data, regularization, or stopping training earlier.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about evaluation metrics, per Lesson 5.
options: On a highly imbalanced dataset, a model that always predicts the majority class can score very high accuracy while catching none of the minority class
Precision measures, of everything flagged as positive, how much actually was positive
Recall and precision always move in the same direction, so improving one automatically improves the other
F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when you want one summary number instead of two
MAE and RMSE are classification metrics, used instead of precision and recall whenever there are more than two classes
questions.explain: A 99%-accurate model that only ever predicts "not fraud" on a 1%-fraud dataset is Lesson 5's own example of why accuracy alone is misleading on imbalanced data. Precision is TP/(TP+FP) — of what was flagged positive, how much actually was. Precision and recall trade off against each other rather than moving together, which is exactly why F1 exists as a harmonic mean balancing both into one number. MAE and RMSE are regression metrics for a continuous output, not classification metrics for more than two classes.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 10, what is the purpose of a loss function in training a model?
options: It converts a prediction's wrongness into a single number that training then tries to minimize
It permanently fixes a model's parameters once training is complete
It decides automatically how many hidden layers a neural network should have
It measures how long training takes to finish, in wall-clock seconds
It replaces the need for a held-out test set, since the loss already tells you how well the model generalizes
It converts categorical features into numeric columns before training begins
questions.explain: Lesson 10 defines a loss function as exactly this: it takes a prediction and the true label and returns a single number, higher meaning worse, which gradient descent then works to reduce. Different loss functions (zero-one, hinge, log loss, and others) penalize the same wrong prediction differently, but all of them exist to turn "wrong" into something trainable.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E is the closest wrong answer because the loss value does come from the same training process, but it is explicitly not a substitute for test-set evaluation — Lesson 11 makes clear that only a genuinely held-out test set, touched once and never used for training decisions, gives an honest measure of generalization. Loss measured during training says nothing trustworthy on its own about how the model performs on new data.

questions.prompt: Per Lessons 7 and 8, a linear SVM scores only 0.88 accuracy on a dataset shaped like two interleaved crescents ("moons"), while a decision tree scores 0.95 on that same data. What explains the gap?
options: A linear model can only draw a straight decision boundary no matter how it's tuned, while a decision tree's stacked single-feature splits can carve out boxy regions that better approximate a curved boundary
The decision tree was trained on more data than the linear SVM in this comparison
Accuracy can't actually be compared between a decision tree and an SVM, since they use different underlying metrics
The linear SVM's score must be a measurement error, since every classifier performs identically on the same dataset
questions.explain: Lesson 7's scikit-learn comparison shows exactly this: a straight-line model like linear SVM genuinely cannot separate two interleaved crescents well, scoring only 0.88, while models that can draw curved or boxy boundaries do much better. Lesson 8 explains why a decision tree's boundary looks boxy — every split tests one feature against one threshold, so stacking splits carves out rectangular regions instead of a smooth curve, which still approximates the crescent shape well enough to reach 0.95.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one gradient descent training step, per Lesson 10, in the correct order.
items: Run the current model forward on a batch of inputs to get predictions
Compute the loss by comparing predictions to the true labels
Compute the gradient — the slope of the loss with respect to each parameter
Nudge every parameter a small step, sized by the learning rate, in the direction that decreases the loss
questions.explain: Lesson 10's training loop runs in exactly this order: a forward pass produces predictions, the loss function scores how wrong they are, the gradient is computed from that loss, and then every parameter is updated by a learning-rate-sized step in the direction that reduces the loss. Repeating this loop, over and over, is what "training" concretely means.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 11, the ________ set is touched only once, at the very end, to report a final honest number — never used to make any decisions along the way.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 draws a sharp line between the validation set (checked repeatedly during development to compare models and tune settings) and the test set, which is touched exactly once, at the end, specifically because repeatedly checking a set and using that feedback to make decisions lets information leak in through the human's choices.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Random Forests and gradient boosting, per Lesson 8.
options: Random Forest trains many trees, each on a random subset of data and features, then averages or votes across them
Gradient boosting builds trees one at a time, each new tree trained specifically to correct the previous trees' errors
A single unconstrained decision tree is one of the harder models to overfit, compared to an ensemble
Ensembles typically improve accuracy and robustness over a single tree, at a real cost to interpretability
A Random Forest's individual trees are all trained on the exact same data and features, which is what lets their errors cancel out
questions.explain: Random Forest trains many trees on random subsets of data and features and combines their predictions; gradient boosting instead builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the last. A single unconstrained tree is actually one of the easiest models to overfit, not one of the harder ones — which is the entire reason ensembles exist. It's specifically the randomness across trees' data/feature subsets, not identical training, that lets individual trees' overfitting quirks cancel out when combined, and that combination comes at a real cost to the easy interpretability a single tree has.

questions.prompt: A developer calls `imputer.fit_transform()` on the full dataset, before splitting into train and test, to fill in missing values. What's wrong with this, per Lessons 12-16?
options: It's train/test contamination — the fill statistic gets learned from test rows too, so test-set information leaks into values used for training
Nothing — fitting the imputer before splitting is the recommended order, since it guarantees train and test see identical fill values
It's fine as long as the imputer uses the mean instead of the median
It's a type mismatch error, since fit_transform requires numeric data that hasn't been split yet
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that any statistic used to fill missing values — like a median — must be learned from the training split only, exactly like Lesson 12's cleaning statistics. Fitting on the full dataset before splitting lets the test set quietly influence a value used during training, which Lesson 16 names directly as train/test contamination, one of its four shapes of data leakage.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: encoding a column like `region` (with no real order) using ________ encoding invents a false numeric relationship — implying region=2 is somehow "between" region=1 and region=3 — that doesn't exist in reality.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 warns specifically against this mistake: ordinal encoding is appropriate only when a real order exists, like low/medium/high. Used on a column with no real order, like region or plan, it invents a false numeric relationship a model may learn spurious patterns from — one-hot encoding is the correct choice there instead.

questions.prompt: Match each situation from Lesson 14 to the strategy it calls for.
left: Only a handful of rows affected, missingness looks random
A column is missing in most rows
A meaningful fraction missing, and missingness itself may be informative
Any imputation statistic, whatever strategy is chosen
right: Must be learned from the training split only, never the full dataset
Drop those rows
Consider dropping the whole column
Impute a reasonable value and add a _was_missing flag column
questions.explain: Lesson 14's decision guide: a few randomly-missing rows can just be dropped; a column missing in most rows is often better dropped entirely; a meaningful fraction where missingness itself might be informative calls for imputing a value plus a _was_missing flag to preserve that signal. Whichever strategy is chosen, the actual fill statistic must always be learned from the training split alone, never the full dataset, to avoid the train/test contamination Lesson 16 names.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the data cleaning checklist from Lesson 12.
options: Disguised missing values like the literal string "N/A" need to be explicitly converted to a real missing-value marker, or they can be mistaken for a category or crash a numeric calculation
An impossible value, like an age of 200, should usually be kept as-is, since the model can tell on its own that it's biologically implausible
Inconsistent capitalization, like "Standard", "standard", and "STANDARD", can cause a single real category to be treated as three different ones
Structural fixes like deduplication and format consistency must wait until after the train/test split
Exact duplicate rows, often from export glitches or double submissions, are one of the specific problems a cleaning pass looks for
questions.explain: Lesson 12's worked example converts the literal string "N/A" into a real missing marker specifically because a model has no way to recognize it as missing otherwise, and it also normalizes "Standard"/"standard"/"STANDARD" into one consistent category, since a model would otherwise treat them as three different categories. A model has no way to know an age of 200 is implausible — it just treats it as data, which is why it needs to be caught during cleaning. Lesson 12 explicitly says structural fixes like deduplication and formatting can happen before splitting; it's specifically statistics learned from the data, like a fill value, that must wait until after the split and be learned from training data only.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a leak-free data preparation pipeline, drawing on Chapter 3's lessons, in the correct order.
items: Fix structural issues in the full dataset — duplicates, inconsistent formatting, impossible values
Split the cleaned data into train and test sets
Fit an imputer and a categorical encoder on the training split only
Apply those same fitted imputer and encoder to transform the test split
questions.explain: Lesson 12 allows structural fixes like deduplication and formatting consistency on the full dataset before splitting, since those don't depend on any statistic computed from the data. Lessons 14 and 15 are explicit that anything learned from the data itself — an imputer's fill value, an encoder's categories — must be fit on the training split only, after splitting, and then applied to transform the test split using those already-learned values, never refit on test rows. Skipping this order is exactly the train/test contamination Lesson 16 names.

questions.prompt: A network stacks three layers, none of which has a nonlinear activation function. Per Lessons 17-18, what does this network actually compute, no matter how many such layers are added?
options: The exact same thing as one single linear layer — stacked linear layers algebraically collapse into one combined weight and bias
A strictly more powerful function than a single layer, since more layers always add more representational power
The same thing as a decision tree, since both are built from simple arithmetic
An error, since a neural network requires at least one activation function to run at all
questions.explain: Lesson 18 proves this by hand: two stacked linear layers, substituted algebraically, produce the exact same output at every input as one combined linear layer with a computed weight and bias. No matter how many purely linear layers are stacked, the whole network can only ever draw a straight line or flat plane — the nonlinear activation function is specifically what prevents this collapse and lets depth add real power.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, what does self-attention let every token in a sequence do that a recurrent neural network's step-by-step hidden state cannot?
options: Compute a direct relationship with every other token at once, with no relay through intermediate steps and no information fading from compression
Skip the need for any numeric computation entirely, relying only on word order
Avoid needing a GPU, since self-attention is cheaper to compute than an RNN's hidden state
Guarantee the model will never make an incorrect prediction once attention is added
Remove the need for positional information entirely, since attention already encodes word order automatically
Train using a completely different algorithm than backpropagation and gradient descent
questions.explain: Lesson 21 explains that self-attention computes a direct dot-product score between every pair of tokens, so a relationship between word 1 and word 500 is exactly as direct as one between word 1 and word 2 — unlike an RNN, where distant information has to survive being compressed through a single carried hidden state across every intermediate step. This also makes every token's calculation independent of the others, which is what enables parallel computation on a GPU.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E sounds plausible because attention does replace the RNN's order-carrying hidden state, but Lesson 21 is explicit that dot products between vectors don't care about order on their own — swapping two tokens' positions leaves their attention scores unchanged unless something else encodes where they sat. That's exactly why transformers have to add positional encoding back in explicitly; attention does not get word order for free.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if a ReLU neuron's weighted sum is negative for every training example it ever sees, it outputs 0 forever and its gradient is also 0 forever — a failure mode called a dead, or dying, ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 names this specific failure mode the dying (or dead) ReLU problem: because ReLU's slope is exactly 0 for any negative input, a neuron stuck outputting 0 for every example also has a gradient of 0, so it stops learning entirely. Sensible weight initialization, reasonable learning rates, and variants like leaky ReLU all reduce how often this happens, but it's a real trade-off that comes with ReLU's simplicity.

questions.prompt: Match each architecture from Lesson 20 to what it's actually built to notice.
right: Relationships between any two positions at once, via self-attention
Nothing structural — every input is treated as independent
Local spatial patterns, via a small kernel reused across every position
Sequential order, via a hidden state carried forward one step at a time
questions.explain: Lesson 20's side-by-side comparison lines these up exactly: a fully connected layer treats every input as independent, with no structural assumption at all. A CNN exploits an image's spatial structure with a small, reused kernel. An RNN exploits a sequence's order by carrying a hidden state forward one step at a time. A transformer replaces that step-by-step carry with self-attention, letting every position relate to every other position directly and in parallel.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about backpropagation, per Lesson 19.
options: Backpropagation is the chain rule from calculus, applied layer by layer, to compute each weight's contribution to the loss
A weight sitting right next to the output needs fewer chained derivatives to compute its gradient than a weight buried in an earlier layer
Backpropagation is a fundamentally different kind of learning algorithm than the gradient descent introduced in Chapter 2
A hand-derived gradient can be checked by nudging a weight slightly and measuring how much the loss actually moves, then comparing to the chain-rule result
Once gradients are computed, the weights are updated by adding the learning rate times the gradient, moving further in the direction of higher loss
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit that backpropagation is not a different kind of learning — it's the chain rule, applied layer by layer, computing exactly the gradients gradient descent (Chapter 2) already knows how to use. The lesson's own worked example needed only two links in the chain for a weight next to the output but four links for a weight further back, because the error has to flow backward through more intermediate steps. It also verifies the chain-rule gradient against a numerical gradient computed by nudging a weight and measuring the loss change — and the actual update subtracts the learning rate times the gradient, moving toward lower loss, not adds it.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 23, what does `pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="...")` actually do under the hood, compared to the two-line AutoTokenizer/AutoModel pattern?
options: It calls from_pretrained for the same tokenizer and model, just wrapped into one call, with pre- and post-processing handled for you
It trains a brand-new model from scratch on the sentiment-analysis task
It skips downloading any files, since pipelines run without needing a model's weights
It only works for models that were never published on the Hugging Face Hub
questions.explain: Lesson 23 is direct about this: pipeline still calls from_pretrained under the hood for both the tokenizer and the model — the exact same download as the explicit two-line pattern — it's just one line shorter, with the pre- and post-processing (turning raw output back into a readable label) handled for you. Reach for the two-line pattern when you need raw hidden states or a custom head; reach for pipeline when a standard task already has one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: setting a parameter's ________ to False tells backpropagation to skip computing a gradient for it entirely, which is how feature extraction freezes a pretrained model's layers while only the new head trains.
questions.explain: Lesson 25 shows this directly in code: setting param.requires_grad = False on the pretrained model's parameters excludes them from the chain rule entirely, so gradient descent never updates them — only the small new classification head, left with requires_grad = True, actually trains. In the lesson's own example this trains roughly 0.0014% of the total parameters.

questions.prompt: Match each model card signal from Lesson 26 to what it tells you.
left: Downloads and Spaces using a model
right: What it's actually built on, and what else shares that base
Does it do the task you need, at all
How it performs on named benchmarks, self-reported by the publisher
Is it actually used and trusted by others
questions.explain: Lesson 26's checklist lines these up exactly: pipeline_tag and tags tell you whether a model does the task you need at all; download counts and the Spaces built on it signal real usage and trust; model-index results show benchmark performance, explicitly self-reported rather than independently audited; and the Finetuned from lineage shows what a model is actually built on, and what else shares that same base.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about choosing between using a model as-is versus fine-tuning it, per Lesson 24.
options: If a model already fine-tuned for your exact task exists and scores well, using it as-is is the right call
If your domain uses specialized language the base model wasn't trained on, like legal or medical jargon, fine-tuning is the better fit
Fine-tuning with very little labeled data is the safest option, since more training is always better
Fine-tuning uses a deliberately small learning rate so the model's existing general-language knowledge isn't destroyed, a failure mode called catastrophic forgetting
Fine-tuning starts from randomly initialized weights, the same as training a new model from scratch
questions.explain: Lesson 24's decision table is explicit: an existing good fine-tune means use it as-is; specialized domain language means fine-tune. With very little labeled data, the table says fine-tuning is risky and overfits fast — as-is or Lesson 25's feature extraction is preferred instead. Fine-tuning deliberately uses a small learning rate (2e-5 in the lesson's example, versus 0.5 for a toy network trained from scratch) specifically to avoid catastrophic forgetting, and it starts from the pretrained model's existing weights, not randomly initialized ones — that's the whole point of starting from a pretrained checkpoint.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of going from a model name to a working prediction, per Lessons 22-23, in the correct order.
items: Search the Hub to find a real model name, like bert-base-uncased
Call AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained and AutoModel.from_pretrained with that same model name
Pass text through the tokenizer to get numeric input IDs
Run those input IDs through the model to get the output hidden states
questions.explain: Lesson 22 covers finding a model on the Hub; Lesson 23 picks up from there — a model name found via search gets passed to AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained and AutoModel.from_pretrained together, the tokenizer turns text into numeric input_ids, and the model then runs those IDs through a forward pass to produce output hidden states, exactly the order the lesson's own code example follows.

questions.code:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
questions.prompt: Lesson 28 splits the capstone's data with this call. What does `stratify=y` specifically guard against?
options: A random split accidentally dumping most of one class into the test set, instead of preserving the same roughly 63/37 benign-to-malignant ratio in both splits
The model memorizing the order the rows appear in the original dataset
The scaler being fit on the test set instead of the training set
The need to set a random_state for reproducibility
questions.explain: Lesson 28 explains that without stratify=y, a random split could accidentally dump most of one class into the test set; stratify=y keeps the same roughly 63/37 benign-to-malignant ratio in both the training and test splits. random_state=42 is a separate, unrelated setting — it just makes the split reproducible, not balanced.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in Lesson 28's capstone, StandardScaler().fit(X_train) is fit on the training rows only, then used to ________ both X_train and X_test — fitting it on the full dataset before splitting would repeat the exact leakage mistake Lesson 16 named.
questions.explain: Lesson 28 applies the exact rule from Chapter 3: the scaler's mean and standard deviation are learned (fit) from the training rows only, then that same already-fitted scaler is used to transform both X_train and X_test. Fitting it on the full dataset before splitting would let test-set statistics leak into values used for training — precisely the train/test contamination Lesson 16 named.

questions.prompt: Lesson 29's capstone confusion matrix for malignant (0) vs. benign (1) is shown above, at 98.2% accuracy. Select every true statement about this result.
options: One real malignant case was predicted benign — the single miss is the costlier kind of mistake in a medical screening context
One benign case was predicted malignant, which means one patient gets an unnecessary follow-up test
The 98.2% accuracy figure alone would hide which of the two kinds of mistake the model actually made
Both kinds of mistake in this matrix are equally costly, so reporting just the overall accuracy is sufficient
The recall of 0.976 for the malignant class is a different measurement than the single missed case in the confusion matrix — they describe unrelated things
questions.explain: Lesson 29 reads the matrix in exactly these human terms: one missed malignant case (predicted benign) is the costlier mistake in a medical screening context, flagged back in Lesson 5 as the error that matters most there; one false alarm (predicted malignant, actually benign) just means an unnecessary follow-up test. A single accuracy number can't say which 2 of 114 predictions were wrong or whether the two kinds of mistake cost the same, which is exactly why the lesson insists on reporting the confusion matrix and per-class recall/precision too — and the 0.976 malignant recall is explicitly the same single miss, just expressed as a rate instead of a raw count, not a different, unrelated number.

questions.prompt: Match each step of the capstone's five-step plan, per Lesson 27, to what happens in it.
right: Fit a StandardScaler and train a LogisticRegression baseline
Accuracy, confusion matrix, precision/recall — read honestly, not cherry-picked
Load the data and understand the target
Run the trained model on data it has never seen
questions.explain: Lesson 27's five-step project plan maps directly to this: step 1 loads the data and understands the target; step 2 fits a StandardScaler and trains a LogisticRegression baseline; step 3 runs that trained model on unseen test data; step 4 evaluates honestly with accuracy, the full confusion matrix, and precision/recall rather than one cherry-picked number. Step 5, Present, closes the plan in Lesson 30.

questions.prompt: Put the capstone's five-step project plan, per Lesson 27, in the correct order.
items: Load the data and understand the target
Fit a StandardScaler and train a LogisticRegression baseline
Run the trained model on data it has never seen
Evaluate honestly with accuracy, confusion matrix, and precision/recall for both classes
Write up the result the way you'd show it in a portfolio
questions.explain: Lesson 27 lays out this exact five-step plan, each step mapping back to an earlier chapter: load and split is features and labels (Lesson 3); scale and train applies train/test discipline (Lesson 11) to a classification baseline (Lessons 6-7); predict runs the trained model on unseen data; evaluate applies Lesson 5's full metric toolkit instead of one cherry-picked number; and present applies the same model-card-style honesty Lesson 26 taught for judging someone else's model, now to your own.
